title: Episode 14 - Sprout Turns Toward the Sun

beats.narration: The last feature. Cy promised investors a Sprout with a rotating base that slowly turns the plant toward the window, so it grows straight instead of leaning.
It will be magical. A plant that dances with the sun.
A plant that dances with the sun needs a motor, a gearbox, a sensor to know where it is pointing, and a lot of current.
And motors are where software meets physics most directly. Things have mass. They overshoot. They get hot. Today, the final piece: making things move.
A brushed DC motor is the simplest. Apply voltage and it spins; reverse the voltage and it spins the other way. More voltage, more speed.
But it has no idea where it is pointing.
A stepper motor moves in precise steps, often two hundred per revolution. Count the steps, and you know the position, as long as it never skips.
A hobby servo has its own controller inside and moves to whatever angle you command.
We are using a small brushed DC motor with a gearbox. Cheap, quiet, and strong enough to turn a pot full of wet soil.
But it needs a sensor to tell us where it is.
Steppers deserve a closer look, because they are everywhere in printers and small machines. Their coils are energized in sequence, and each change pulls the shaft one step around.
Change the coils faster, and it spins faster. Stop, and it holds position firmly, as long as the coils stay powered.
That holding costs current even when nothing moves, which is a poor fit for a battery device.
And if you ask a stepper to accelerate too quickly, or push against too much load, it skips steps. Without a sensor, the code never knows.
It simply believes the wrong position from then on.
Which is why steppers usually find a home switch at startup: they turn until a switch clicks, and call that position zero. Then they count from there.
An encoder measures rotation. Sprout's is a small magnetic disc on the motor shaft, with two sensors that produce pulses as it turns.
There are two signals, A and B, offset by a quarter of a cycle. That offset is the clever part.
If A rises while B is low, the shaft is turning one way. If A rises while B is high, it is turning the other way.
This is called quadrature. By counting every edge of both signals, the code tracks both position and direction.
Many microcontrollers have timers that decode quadrature in hardware, so not a single pulse is missed.
Our encoder gives twelve pulses per motor turn, times four edges, times a gearbox of one hundred fifty. That is seven thousand two hundred counts per turn of the pot.

beats.narration: A microcontroller pin cannot power a motor directly. The motor needs far more current than a pin can supply, and it creates electrical spikes that would destroy the chip.
Between them sits an H-bridge: four switches arranged so the motor can be connected either way round. Close one diagonal pair, and current flows forward.
Close the other, and it flows backward.
Speed comes from PWM, exactly as with the pump. The duty cycle sets the average voltage the motor sees.
And the encoder closes the loop, telling the code what actually happened.
And never, ever close both switches on the same side at once. That shorts the power supply straight to ground, through the bridge. People call it shoot-through.
The bridge calls it its last day.
Good driver chips prevent that internally, and add a short dead time when switching direction. Use one.
Do not build an H-bridge from loose parts unless you enjoy the smell of hot silicon.
Now the hard part. Ada wants the pot to turn to exactly ninety degrees. The simplest approach: turn the motor on, watch the encoder, and switch off at ninety.
The pot is heavy, so it coasts past the target. The code reverses. It overshoots the other way. Back and forth, never settling. The plant gets seasick.
The classic solution is a PID controller: proportional, integral, derivative. Three simple terms that together produce smooth, accurate control.
The proportional term pushes harder the farther away we are. Far from target, full power. Close, gentle. Alone, it often settles slightly short, because friction balances the small push.

visual.title: The three terms of PID
items: P: push in proportion to the error
I: push harder if error lingers over time
D: brake when error is shrinking fast

beats.narration: The integral term adds up the error over time. If a small error lingers, the integral grows until it pushes through the friction.

visual.title: The three terms of PID

beats.narration: The derivative term watches how fast the error is changing and brakes as the target approaches, preventing overshoot.

beats.narration: Notice the integral is clamped. Otherwise, if the motor is blocked for a while, the integral grows enormous, and when released, the motor charges past the target.

visual.title: A simple PID step, called at a fixed rate
lines: int32_t deriv = err - last_err;  last_err = err;
>int32_t out = (KP * err + KI * integral + KD * deriv) / SCALE;

beats.narration: That is called windup.

beats.narration: And the controller runs at a fixed rate, from a timer, using integer math. Irregular timing makes the derivative and integral terms meaningless.

beats.narration: The three gains, how much of each term to apply, must be tuned for the actual mechanism. Ben and Ada start simple.
The last step matters most. A controller tuned for an empty pot may oscillate with a full one. Test across the whole range of real conditions.

visual.title: A practical tuning recipe
items: Start with I and D at zero
Raise P until it responds briskly, with a little overshoot
Add D to calm the overshoot
Add a small I to remove the final error
Test with a light pot and a heavy, wet pot

beats.narration: It turns, it slows, it stops at ninety. Gerald is facing the window!

beats.narration: Even with good control, jumping straight from stopped to full speed is harsh. Soil sloshes, gears wear, and the current spike drains the battery. So the target itself moves smoothly.
A trapezoidal profile accelerates gently, cruises at a steady speed, then decelerates gently into the final position.
Instead of telling the controller go to ninety degrees, we feed it a sequence of moving targets along that curve.
Smoother profiles, with gradual changes in acceleration too, reduce vibration even further. For a slowly rotating plant, the trapezoid is plenty.
And it means the motor never draws its full stall current. The battery thanks us.
The prototype works. Then reality arrives, one surprise at a time. Ada keeps a list on the whiteboard.
Motors are electrically noisy. Their brushes spark, and their current changes suddenly. That noise can reset the microcontroller or corrupt sensor readings.

visual.title: Motor lessons, learned the hard way
items: Motors make electrical noise: filter and separate grounds
Switching off a motor creates a voltage spike
Stall current can be many times running current
Heat builds slowly; protect against it
Gears have backlash; position has slack
Mechanics wear; the tuning drifts
Always have a way to stop

beats.narration: Separate the motor's power path, add filtering, and keep its wires away from the soil probe.

beats.narration: Autumn. The factory line hums. Bootloaders are programmed, keys injected, self tests pass. Five thousand Sprouts, each with a rotating base, go into boxes.
When we started, we had a fern, a soldering iron, and a lot of confidence. Now we have a product. Every episode, every lesson, is in there somewhere.

beats.narration: Over fourteen episodes, we followed one small product from idea to shipping. We drew the map before building. We brought up hardware carefully, and learned to read datasheets and schematics.
